newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Mexico working to settle tomato squabble.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Mexico working to settle tomato squabble.

text.p: Commerce Department officials were meeting Wednesday with Mexican tomato growers to try to resolve a bitter fight over tomato imports and avert a potentially ugly trade war.
"Right now the parties are negotiating in good faith to reach a settlement," said Commerce Department spokesperson Anne Luzzatto.

The officials are trying to come up with a so-called "suspension agreement" that would end a controversial trade complaint brought by Florida tomato growers against Mexico for allegedly dumping produce in the United States at cheap prices and costing U.S. growers millions of dollars in lost sales.

The dispute between the two big trading partners has been a particularly bitter issue, with Mexico threatening to retaliate against a host of high-value, high-volume agricultural imports from the United States if Washington imposes sanctions on imports of Mexican tomatoes.

The Commerce Department was expected to release a key ruling Tuesday in the complaint process on whether or not it agreed with the U.S. industry's position that Mexico is dumping its produce, and at what levels.
However, the agency said it was delaying its decision until no later than Oct. 28 to give it more time to study all the issues raised by both sides.
Informed sources said a key reason for the extension was to arrive at a face-saving compromise that would settle the issue and allow both parties to walk away relatively happy.

"This is a very important delay that could lead to a very successful conclusion on everyone's part," said Al Tank, vice president of the National Pork Producers Council. The pork producers group and other major commodity groups have been strongly against the complaint due to fears that the dispute will hurt trade with Mexico.

Various options are being talked about in a suspension agreement, according to informed sources, with most of the discussion currently centred on establishing a price floor for imports from Mexico. No quantity limitations are believed to be under discussion.

Although U.S. growers are not at the negotiating table, the Florida industry appears to be having an active imput in the process. One congressional source said a compromise proposal was drafted a few days ago and was sent to the Florida growers for review.

Officials with the Florida Fruit & Vegetable Association, which spearheaded the drive on behalf of the domestic industry, would not discuss specifics of any proposals being considered, but said they have always been open to different approaches to settle the fight.

"We have never wanted to take the Mexicans out of the market," said Mike Stuart of the Florida association. "What we want is a level playing field ... we have not excluded any avenue for settlement of this."
